paragraphs: One-sentence judgment: this occupation is worth further verification only if you are willing to accept long medical education and residency training, continuously handle neurological disease that comes with incomplete information and serious consequences between outpatient and inpatient settings, and write every judgment into reviewable charts and communication records.

Core output: turning history, neurological examination, laboratory and imaging results, medication responses, and follow-up into traceable diagnostic and treatment records: differential diagnosis, treatment plans, risk communication, referrals, and multidisciplinary handover, rather than only a conclusion.

20 to 120 minute safe trial: use a fictional case for one non-clinical exercise: organize the chief complaint and the illness timeline, list the key points of the neurological examination, and write out three reasons why imaging or electrophysiology is needed and two red flags that must be escalated immediately; do not make diagnoses or treatment recommendations for any real patient on this basis.

First threshold: first confirm the authorization boundaries: who may make diagnoses, prescribe, interpret imaging, sign reports, and determine brain death. The United States requires a state medical license and institutional authorization, while mainland China requires physician qualifications, practice registration, and practice within the registered scope; technical, research, and assistant roles do not obtain these authorities.

Neurologists (O*NET-SOC 29-1217.00) diagnose, manage, and treat diseases and disorders of the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves non-surgically: interviewing to collect history and family history, completing neurological examinations, ordering and interpreting laboratory and neuroimaging studies, making diagnoses, developing and adjusting treatment plans, and monitoring medication responses.

entries: History and neurological examination: interview to collect the chief complaint, symptoms, past history, and family history, and examine consciousness, cranial nerves, motor function, sensation, reflexes, coordination, language, and cognitive function.

Testing and imaging interpretation: order and interpret lumbar puncture, EEG, electromyography, nerve conduction velocity, blood and cerebrospinal fluid analysis, and neuroimaging such as MRI, SPECT, and PET.

Diagnosis and treatment decisions: synthesize history and test results to reach a neurological diagnosis, prescribe or administer medications and monitor behavioral and cognitive adverse effects, and when necessary use treatments such as transcranial magnetic stimulation, vagus nerve stimulation, or deep brain stimulation.

Communication and shared decision making: explain the diagnosis, prognosis, and the benefits, risks, and costs of each option to patients and families, and provide counseling on risk factors and genetic or environmental issues.

Collaboration, referral, and records: coordinate neurological services with other medical team activities, refer when necessary, arrange supportive care such as physical therapy, specialized nursing, and social services, maintain charts, and take part in continuing education and research.

Teaching, training, and quality management: provide training for medical students and staff, supervise medical technologists performing neurodiagnostic or treatment activities, and take part in quality improvement, continuing education, and neuroscience research.

paragraphs: The work is mainly outpatient clinics, inpatient wards, and consultations, and is almost entirely indoors; the O*NET work context shows 100% need face-to-face discussions daily, 98% consider precision or accuracy extremely important, 92% work more than 40 hours per week, and 91% have a regular schedule.

Decision responsibility is highly concentrated: O*NET shows that 92% report a great deal of decision freedom, while 75% consider the consequences of error extremely serious and 57% carry very high responsibility for the health and safety of others, so verification, review, and record requirements are not relaxed by seniority.

Quality is measured by traceable diagnostic reasoning, evidence-based test and imaging interpretation, monitored medication adverse effects, patients and families understanding the plan, and complete handover records, rather than by the speed of seeing patients.

The work loop in order is: collect history and examine → order and interpret tests and imaging → form a diagnosis and differential → develop and adjust treatment and monitor responses → communicate, refer, and hand over across disciplines → record and follow up; occupational boundary: this occupation is not the same as neurosurgeons, clinical neuropsychologists, or neuroelectrophysiology technologists, and surgery, psychometric, and technical operation authority and training paths differ.

Neurosurgeons: handle surgical problems of the brain, spine, and peripheral nerves and carry surgical decisions and perioperative responsibility; this occupation is mainly non-surgical diagnosis and treatment, and the two have different training paths and scopes of responsibility.

Clinical neuropsychologists: issue reports based on standardized cognitive and psychological assessment and do not take on medication prescribing or medical treatment of neurological disease; neuroelectrophysiology technologists perform examination operations and technical records and do not make diagnoses or sign reports.

Selection signal: do not compare only that all handle neurological disease; compare whether there is surgical authority, whether psychometric reports are issued, who makes diagnosis and prescribing decisions, and what supervision and scope-of-practice limits apply.
Centered on surgical decisions and procedures, carrying surgical risk and perioperative responsibility, without the long-term non-surgical medication management of this occupation.
Compare this direction if you prefer carrying surgical procedures and perioperative decisions and are willing to complete long-term surgical training.

Break down the tasks first: generative AI task exposure is not equal to actual adoption, automation probability, or job disappearance; this page uses only O*NET 29-1217.00 tasks and work context for item-by-item analysis and does not invent a replacement rate for this occupation.

Editorial scenario (subject to authorization, de-identification, and manual verification): better suited for assistance: draft chart summaries, verification of test and medication lists, differential diagnosis prompt lists, draft patient education materials, and organizing follow-up questions.

Editorial scenario (subject to authorization, de-identification, and manual verification): retrieval assistance: can help form search strings and organize guideline or literature candidates; citations, versions, study design, applicable populations, and strength of conclusions must be manually verified.

Editorial scenario: organize manually confirmed imaging descriptions and medication lists and check for missing fields; no AI candidate lesion or drug interaction recognition performance data was obtained this round, and text assistance is not substituted for clinical screening.

Must not be delegated to AI: making neurological diagnoses, prescribing or adjusting medications, determining brain death, interpreting imaging conclusions, or deciding whether to continue testing or delay referral.

Human control points: verify patient identity and source materials, confirm indications, contraindications, and interactions, state the scope of practice, have a licensed person sign, and carry out emergency escalation.

Data threshold: process the minimum necessary patient information only in authorized systems; imaging, EEG, and chart materials must not be entered into unauthorized external models or tools, and privacy and audit rules must be followed.
Editorial exercise: accumulate supervised records of history taking, examination, interpretation, shared decision making, and handover; do not claim it outperforms the speed of generating text.

Name and scope: neurologists correspond to O*NET-SOC 29-1217.00 (Neurologists, non-surgical). The corresponding clinical position in mainland China is a hospital neurology department physician; the Physicians Law of the People's Republic of China requires lawfully obtaining physician qualifications, obtaining a physician practice certificate through registration, and practicing according to the registered practice location, category, and scope. The Chinese language page does not prove that the two classifications can be equated.

Scope comparison: the National Bureau of Statistics of China publishes average wages of urban unit employees by industry category and does not list neurology department physicians or neurologists separately, so this page only uses the health and social work industry category average as a reference.

Checkable reference: in 2025 the average annual wage of employed persons in the health and social work industry was 146,266 yuan for urban non-private units and 75,631 yuan for urban private units in the same category; the statistical scope is legal entities with 5 or more employees in urban areas, and the survey excludes self-employed individuals and freelancers.

Insufficient evidence: no national Chinese occupational wage distribution under the same scope was obtained this round, and industry averages cannot infer physician percentiles or individual income. Qualification, residency training, professional titles, and specialty training are verified separately; the 2016 specialty training document was a system pilot, and the usual 2—4 years cannot be generalized to all current neurology positions as a uniform requirement. The 2026 catalog lists neurology 308 at the intermediate level, and other levels follow the current year's local rules.

The 2025 BLS OEWS data shown by O*NET use the exact occupation 29-1217.00 Neurologists scope: a median hourly wage of 119.50 USD and median annual wage of 248,560 USD; that scope is not entry pay or a personal quote.

The national percentile annual wages under the same scope are: 10th percentile 83,370 USD, 25th percentile 155,990 USD, 75th percentile 357,990 USD, and 90th percentile 450,780 USD; corresponding hourly rates 40.08, 75.00, 172.11, and 216.72 USD.
Percentiles and the median all use the 2025 BLS OEWS national scope and cannot be directly compared across years, regions, or specialties.

OEWS is an employee wage statistic and excludes self-employment and partnership income; items such as on-call duty, consultations, academic appointments, and overtime must be verified against the statistical definitions and specific quotes, and it cannot be said across the board that none of them are reflected.
A low percentile is not a resident or new entrant starting salary, and distribution data cannot be used to estimate individual take-home pay or after-tax income.

Scheduling, on-call duty, and performance structures at academic medical centers, private hospitals, and specialty clinics change actual income, and should be verified against the specific employer, region, and position level; United States figures cannot be converted into individual income in mainland China.

paragraphs: Caution signal (editorial observation): medical education, supervised training, licensure, and continuous learning requirements demand serious commitment; ABPN specialty certification is not uniform legal entry, so verify per employer and institution requirements.

Verification method: personality labels cannot determine fit; use fictional cases to complete history structuring, differential diagnosis, and risk communication exercises, and be evaluated by licensed clinical staff in a compliant teaching environment.

Boundary statement: this list cannot replace institutional diagnostic and treatment standards, infection control, privacy, and patient safety requirements. The main risks are concentrated in evidence gaps and delayed escalation in diagnostic reasoning, errors in imaging and test interpretation, medication adverse effects and interactions, insufficient informed communication, and information loss in cross-professional handover; control requirements should be tailored to the organization's scope.

Direct answer: the main risks in this occupation are converging on conclusions too early with insufficient evidence, errors in imaging or electrophysiology interpretation, unmonitored medication adverse effects, red flags not escalated in time, and information loss in cross-professional handover; control depends on structured charts, clear escalation thresholds, peer review, and closed-loop follow-up.

The United States survey shows 75% extremely serious error consequences, 98% rating precision as extremely important, 57% with very high health and safety responsibility, and 57% with daily disease exposure, which support the risk premise rather than an incidence rate. ABPN training requirements do not prove the effectiveness of each control measure; the controls are editorial suggestions tailored to institutional standards.

Affected roles: neurologists responsible for outpatient, emergency, and inpatient treatment decisions, test and imaging interpretation, prescribing and medication monitoring, and on-call consultation, and the nursing, imaging, and neuroelectrophysiology teams involved in their handovers; the consequences of error are equally serious during training, so supervision and review requirements are not relaxed by seniority.

Possible consequences: delayed or wrong diagnosis causes irreversible neurological damage and missed treatment windows; medication-related adverse events may be life-threatening; missing handover or records leads to repeat testing and untraceable responsibility.

Step 0: determine the practice jurisdiction and authorization scope. First clarify the country or region where you plan to practice, and find out the protected titles, medical education, graduate medical training, licensure, specialty certification, and continuing certification requirements; the path on this page is an editorial synthesis, does not represent uniform entry conditions, and does not constitute any diagnosis, prescribing, or signing authorization.

Complete history taking, neurological examination, chart writing, test ordering, and result interpretation in a supervised environment, and accept clinical skills assessment and preceptor feedback, rather than making independent diagnostic or treatment decisions for real patients.
Supervised clinical training

During residency, take on the initial diagnosis and management of common neurological diseases, identify cases requiring escalation or transfer, and complete clinical skills assessments and rotation requirements as required.
Residents take on-call duty and management within the training permit, supervision, and institutional release scope

After obtaining the applicable license and institutional authority, take on diagnosis and treatment; specialty certification is verified per employer and institution requirements, and ABPN is not treated as a uniform independent practice legal prerequisite.
Independent practice and specialty direction

Take part in subspecialty directions (epilepsy, cerebrovascular disease, neuromuscular, sleep, neurocritical care, and others), mentoring, quality improvement, and clinical research, and be responsible for processes and training.

entries.answer: According to O*NET 29-1217.00, this occupation diagnoses, manages, and treats diseases and disorders of the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves non-surgically: interviewing to collect history and family history, completing neurological examinations, ordering and interpreting laboratory and electrophysiological tests and neuroimaging such as MRI, SPECT, and PET, making diagnoses, prescribing and monitoring medication responses, developing and adjusting treatment plans, determining brain death, coordinating supportive care, referring when necessary, and communicating and recording with the multidisciplinary team.
entries.question: What do neurologists do every day?

entries.answer: Neurosurgeons handle surgical problems of the brain, spine, and peripheral nerves and carry surgical and perioperative responsibility; clinical neuropsychologists issue reports based on standardized cognitive and psychological assessment and do not take on medication prescribing and medical treatment; neuroelectrophysiology technologists perform examination operations and organize technical data and do not make diagnoses or sign reports. This occupation centers on non-surgical diagnosis and treatment and long-term medication management, and classification proximity does not mean qualifications and authority are interchangeable.
entries.question: How does it differ from neurosurgeons and clinical neuropsychologists?

entries.answer: Suited to people who can build a structured differential framework when information is incomplete, are willing to complete a systematic and repetitive neurological examination, can explain uncertainty and risk clearly, are willing to record and accept peer review, and can carry the on-call and decision pressure created by serious error consequences; interest codes or personality labels cannot determine fit or hiring.
entries.question: What kind of people are suited?

entries.answer: The available evidence does not support a replacement conclusion: O*NET does not provide a generative AI adoption or automation rate for this occupation. Tools are more likely to change chart summaries, checklist verification, materials retrieval, and draft patient education materials first, while diagnostic judgments, prescribing and adjustment, imaging conclusions, brain death determination, and emergency decisions still need to be borne by qualified and registered physicians.
entries.question: Will AI replace this occupation?

entries.answer: Any summary, triage prompt, imaging candidate, or interaction prompt must be checked against the original records, complete images, medication lists, and test timing, and reviewed by licensed clinical staff; tool output cannot become an automatic diagnosis or treatment instruction.

entries.answer: There is no national occupational wage distribution precisely corresponding to this occupation. The National Bureau of Statistics of China publishes by industry category for 2025: the average annual wage in the health and social work industry was 146,266 yuan for urban non-private units and 75,631 yuan for urban private units; this is an industry average that excludes self-employed individuals and freelancers and cannot be interpreted as starting pay or percentiles for this position.

entries.answer: The 2025 BLS OEWS shown by O*NET uses the 29-1217.00 exact occupation scope: a median hourly wage of 119.50 USD and median annual wage of 248,560 USD, with annual wage percentiles of 83,370—450,780 USD; that survey excludes self-employment and partnership income and does not reflect the compensation structure of on-call duty and academic appointments, so it cannot be treated as individual take-home income.
entries.question: How should the United States wage data be read?

entries.answer: O*NET classifies this occupation as Job Zone 5 (SVP 8.0 and above), and the education survey shows 64% postdoctoral, 29% doctorate, and 5% master's. The common United States path is a medical school degree (MD or DO), neurology residency training in an ACGME-accredited program (PGY-1 one year plus three years), a medical license issued separately by each state medical board, and ABPN specialty certification; license and certification requirements differ by state, and specialty certification is a voluntary professional credential that does not constitute a uniform national threshold. In mainland China, physician qualifications must be obtained and registered under the Physicians Law, and residency and specialty standardized training are usually required.
entries.question: What education and certification are needed?

entries.answer: The Physicians Law of the People's Republic of China requires lawfully obtaining physician qualifications, obtaining a physician practice certificate through registration, and practicing according to the registered practice location, category, and scope. Clinical training usually includes standardized residency training and standardized specialty training (generally 2—4 years according to specialty standards), and intermediate and above professional titles use a unified national examination system; specific conditions follow the current year's national and local health authority announcements.
entries.question: How do you become a neurology department physician in mainland China?

entries.answer: The O*NET work context shows 92% work more than 40 hours per week and 91% have a regular schedule, 75% consider the consequences of error extremely serious, and 98% consider precision extremely important; outpatient and emergency care, consultations, and inpatient on-call duty bring nighttime and weekend work.

career_path_block.direct_answer: First verify medical education, training, licensure, and institutional authority in the work jurisdiction. ABPN adult neurology certification requires PGY-1 one year and the subsequent three years of ACGME neurology training, clinical skills assessments, and examinations; these are certification conditions, not licensure conditions in all states. Chinese physician qualifications and registration, residency training, professional titles, and specialty training are verified separately, and the 2016 pilot's general 2—4 years is not extrapolated to all positions.

locale_requirements.credential_boundary: A medical degree, graduate medical training, a state medical license, ABPN specialty certification, and institutional authorization are different statuses; specialty certification is a voluntary professional credential and does not replace licensure and institutional authorization. In China it is also necessary to distinguish physician qualifications from practice registration; qualifications for other health technical positions are not equal to diagnostic and prescribing authority.
locale_requirements.jurisdiction: The occupational facts on this page use the United States O*NET 29-1217.00 scope; United States licensure and certification reference state medical boards, ABPN, and ACGME; Chinese qualifications and training reference the Physicians Law of the People's Republic of China and the National Health Commission's standardized residency and specialty physician training policies. Other jurisdictions and institutional requirements must be checked against current regulations and systems.
locale_requirements.summary: The O*NET education survey shows 64% postdoctoral training, 29% doctorate, and 5% master's, and a master's alone does not grant a license. ABPN adult certification requires one PGY-1 year plus three years of neurology, with five clinical skills assessments; United States state licensure and certification differ, and the 2016 Chinese specialty training pilot must be verified against currently applicable programs.

personality_fit_block.boundary: The fit signals and tool notes on this page are for self-exploration only and do not constitute capability assessment, selection criteria, practice authorization, or a hiring promise; see the notes below for the evidence positioning of interest and personality frameworks.
personality_fit_block.direct_answer: The key signals for fit with this occupation are: able to build a structured differential framework when information is incomplete, willing to complete a systematic and repetitive neurological examination, able to explain uncertainty clearly, willing to record and accept peer review, and able to carry the on-call and decision pressure created by serious error consequences.

questions.answer: History structuring, neurological examination, test and imaging interpretation, evidence grading, medication monitoring, risk communication, and handover records.
questions.question: What capabilities are mainly needed to do this occupation?

questions.answer: No; the interest code only describes activity preferences, and fit should be judged from supervised training performance, preceptor feedback, and assessment results.
questions.question: Can the IS interest code determine whether I am suited?

questions.answer: O*NET classifies this occupation as Job Zone 5, and the education survey shows 64% postdoctoral, 29% doctorate, and 5% master's; the actual United States path is a medical school degree, ACGME-accredited residency training, and licensure.
questions.question: What education is needed?

questions.answer: In the United States, a state medical license is the legal prerequisite and ABPN neurology specialty certification is a voluntary professional credential; mainland China requires physician qualifications and practice registration, and residents may take part in standardized residency and specialty physician training.
questions.question: Which certifications are needed?

questions.answer: A non-medical background cannot directly provide independent diagnosis and treatment; medical education, training, and licensure in the jurisdiction must be met, and the required education path can be completed anew, so it cannot be asserted that one can only ever work in support roles.
questions.question: Can I transfer in without a medical major?

questions.answer: The O*NET work context shows 92% work more than 40 hours per week and 91% have a regular schedule; outpatient and emergency care, consultations, and inpatient on-call duty bring nighttime and weekend work.
questions.question: Is there much on-call and overtime work?

questions.answer: Decision pressure under extremely serious error consequences, long face-to-face communication, the repetitiveness of examinations, and continuous learning and certification maintenance requirements.
questions.question: Which factors in the work strongly affect fit?

questions.answer: Keep supervised training evaluations, clinical skills assessment records, case and complication review records, and continuing education and certification records.

eeat_signals.source: The partial United States wages for 2025 use the national quintiles verified from the state wage page's United States row, the BLS projection 2025—2035 uses the exact 6.4%, and the O*NET classification 5%—6% is kept separate; the industry detail is 2025. components.work_context_block: Work context: mainly outpatient clinics, inpatient wards, and consultations, and almost entirely indoors; the O*NET work context shows 100% need face-to-face discussions daily, 98% consider precision or accuracy extremely important, 92% work more than 40 hours per week with 91% on a regular schedule, and 75% consider the consequences of error extremely serious. Quality is measured by traceable diagnostic reasoning, evidence-based interpretation, monitored adverse effects, and complete handover records.

description.text: Neurologists (O*NET 29-1217.00) diagnose, manage, and treat diseases and disorders of the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves non-surgically: interviewing to collect history, completing neurological examinations, ordering and interpreting laboratory and neuroimaging studies, making diagnoses, developing and adjusting treatment plans, monitoring medication adverse effects, determining brain death, coordinating supportive care and referrals, and recording communication. This page uses only official sources to explain the occupation scope, tasks, preparation requirements, Chinese and United States statistical scopes, and authorization boundaries.

subject.name: Neurologists
subject.summary: Neurologists (O*NET-SOC 29-1217.00) diagnose, manage, and treat diseases and disorders of the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves non-surgically: collecting history and family history, completing neurological examinations, ordering and interpreting laboratory and neuroimaging studies, making a differential diagnosis, developing and adjusting treatment plans, monitoring medication adverse effects, determining brain death, arranging supportive care and referrals, and communicating and recording with the multidisciplinary team. This page uses only official sources to explain the occupation scope, tasks, preparation requirements, Chinese and United States statistical scopes, and authorization boundaries.
